title: Ratio and scale factors
transcript: A ratio compares amounts measured in consistent units. To keep the same ratio, multiply or divide all the parts by the same factor. A proportion of the whole uses the sum of the ratio parts. A transfer changes the parts while leaving that whole fixed.

In AMC practice, look for scale drawings, recipes, or quantities mixed in the same proportion. Check that the units agree. In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, the ratio can change after something moves. Look for a total that stays constant.
One mixture uses four red beads for every seven blue beads. Find the quantities for five identical batches. Which scale factor applies to each count?
Multiply the red count and the blue count by five. That preserves the comparison per batch. The new counts are twenty reds and thirty-five blues. Dividing both by five recovers the original ratio.
On a one to five hundred drawing, a wall is six centimetres long. Find the actual wall length in metres. First decide what one centimetre on the drawing represents.

One centimetre represents five hundred centimetres. Multiply by six to get the real length in centimetres. There are one hundred centimetres in one metre. Divide the centimetre result by one hundred. The length is thirty metres. The factor from drawing to real length is the same before converting units.
A box initially has red and blue counters in ratio six to two. Move thirty-two from the red pile to the blue pile. The new ratio is two to six. How many counters are there in all?

The total stays the same. In both ratios there are eight equal parts of that same total. Blue goes from two parts to six parts. That increase of four parts consists of exactly the thirty-two transferred counters. One part is eight. Multiply by the full eight parts. The box contains sixty-four counters.

The original piles have forty-eight and sixteen. The transfer changes them to sixteen and forty-eight. Reduce both pairs by the same part size. The two given ratios return, and the total is unchanged.

Multiplying just one ratio term changes the comparison. Apply the same scale factor to every term. When you need a fraction of the whole, add both ratio terms first. A three to five ratio gives three eighths for the first group.

Check that both sides use consistent units before calculating. Name one ratio part and write what it represents. For a change from one ratio to another, identify what stays fixed. Compare the same fraction of that fixed quantity.
